Banded jewelfish Hemichromis fasciatus exhibits a notably extended reproductive life history compared to many other cichlids of similar body size. Egg diameters ranging from 0.8 to 1.53 millimeters give rise to hatchlings with a remarkably small wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0011 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0011 grams], a value reflecting the early stage of development at which the chorion ruptures and the yolk-sac larva emerges. These newly emerged larvae are entirely lecithotrophic, absorbing yolk nutrients before the onset of exogenous feeding. Field surveys conducted in West African river systems indicate that individuals attain a total length at puberty of 8 centimeters [Lp = 8 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to the initiation of gonadal recrudescence and the first observable signs of gametogenesis onset. This length represents a substantial portion of the species ultimate total length, which reaches 26.5 centimeters [Li = 26.5 centimeters] in the largest specimens examined. The growth trajectory between these two size benchmarks is characterized by a rapid phase of mass gain, particularly during the juvenile and sub-adult stages when feeding intensity is highest.

Reproductive investment in Hemichromis fasciatus scales predictably with body size, as demonstrated by length-weight relationships derived from museum specimen series. At the onset of puberty, when individuals first attain a total length of 8 cm [Lp = 8 cm], the corresponding wet weight at puberty is estimated at 7.3 grams [Wwp = 7.3 grams], a body mass that supports the initial development of gonadal tissues and the energetic demands of vitellogenesis. In contrast, fully grown adults that have approached their asymptotic length achieve a substantially greater body mass, with the ultimate wet weight recorded at 255 grams [Wwi = 255 grams] for the largest individuals. This more than thirty-fold increase in mass from puberty to adulthood reflects not only continued somatic growth but also the accumulation of lipid reserves necessary to sustain multiple spawning events across an extended breeding season. Comparisons with congeneric species suggest that these mass-at-length values are consistent with a moderately slow life-history pace typical of cichlids inhabiting seasonally fluctuating freshwater environments.

The environmental temperature regime plays a critical role in shaping the life span and overall physiological performance of Hemichromis fasciatus populations. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant water temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], individuals have been documented to live for as long as 2190 days [am = 2190 days], which corresponds to approximately six years of age. This longevity is notably protracted relative to many small-bodied cichlids, which typically complete their life cycles within two to four years in natural habitats. The extended life span observed at this thermal regime likely reflects a combination of factors, including reduced metabolic costs at moderate temperatures, the absence of predation pressure in captivity, and the species inherent iteroparous reproductive strategy that permits repeated spawning across multiple breeding seasons. Field-based mark-recapture studies in the Niger River basin have produced maximum longevity estimates broadly consistent with these laboratory findings, though natural mortality from predation and seasonal environmental stressors truncates the realized life span for most wild individuals.

Reproductive allocation in this species follows a clear biphasic pattern linked to body size thresholds. Once an individual surpasses the size benchmark of 8 centimeters [Lp = 8 centimeters] total length at puberty, the corresponding wet weight at puberty of 7.3 grams [Wwp = 7.3 grams] marks the point at which reproductive activation begins, with females initiating vitellogenesis and males commencing spermiation. However, the full expression of reproductive potential is not realized until individuals approach their ultimate total length of 26.5 cm [Li = 26.5 cm] and achieve the associated ultimate wet weight of 255 g [Wwi = 255 g]. Gravid females at this terminal size produce substantially larger clutches than their smaller counterparts, a pattern consistent with the positive allometry between maternal body mass and fecundity documented across many cichlid lineages. The ability to defer reproduction until reaching a larger body size confers clear fitness advantages, as larger individuals can guard their nesting territories more effectively and provide more intensive parental care to both eggs and free-swimming fry.

The parental care behavior characteristic of this species, which includes nest guarding and fry tending by both sexes, may also contribute to its relatively extended life span by reducing the energetic costs associated with repeated spawning attempts in a single breeding season.
